extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars and newsroom professionals (editors/reporters/news managers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for organizing newsroom work: classifying events (spot/developing/continuing/what-a-story), allocating personnel and technology over time, and exercising professionalism and flexibility to produce news under routine and emergency conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance preparation for recurring/continuing stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual 'February stories' (e.g., Lincoln/Washington birthdays, Valentine's Day) and other continuing-news items may be assigned days in advance so that 'specific information to be included in the story may be gathered, written, and edited days before its eventual dissemination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prescheduling to conserve personnel and retain control of flow; prepare copy and editing ahead of event; treat continuing stories as predictable series that free staff to handle unforeseen events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign same reporter to hard and soft angles to conserve resources
rubrics_metrics.description: When an unscheduled event (e.g., a fire) has both a hard-news aspect and a soft/feature angle, 'the same person generally reports both the hard-news fire and its soft-news angle, so that the news organization can conserve reporters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine assignments to reduce personnel expenditure rather than splitting coverage between multiple reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot news: rapid-response handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot-news events are 'unscheduled; they appear suddenly and must be processed quickly' and are the 'specifically unforeseen event-as-news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate inability to predict specifics (where/when). Allocate resources immediately; options include paying overtime, pulling staff from other stories, hiring freelancers, reassigning non-report staff (e.g., newswriter as reporter) — choice depends on dispersion of crews and time/space constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain standby staffing for low-probability/high-impact spot events
rubrics_metrics.description: Some spot-news possibilities are so important that organizations 'try to create a stable social arrangement to anticipate them' (e.g., staffed city desk around the clock, twenty-four-hour coverage of the president).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create standing assignments (overnight city desk, dedicated beats) so immediate reallocation is possible without delay; accepts extended resource allocation for rare but critical events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology shapes typifications and allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different news technologies have varying time rhythms (e.g., 'Film can be shot, edited, and aired in an hour; print technology is more cumbersome and time consuming'), and technology 'influences the organization of work' and how events are typified (spot vs developing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess events relative to medium: faster electronic media may treat an event as spot news while print may call it developing; resource plans must reflect medium-specific rhythms and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing news: continuous revision and reconstruction of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing news concerns 'emergent situations' where initial facts are incomplete or reconstructed — 'Most spot-news stories are developing news' and 'as more information becomes known, the "facts" will be more "accurate."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect ongoing updates, repeated editing, resets of formats/headlines; plan for successive bulletins, hold-or-run decisions across editions, and competition with faster media (e.g., television breaking a speech first).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing news: prescheduled series permitting prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing news is 'a series of stories on the same subject based upon events occurring over a period of time' (e.g., a legislative bill's progress) and is 'prescheduled' so reporters can predict and plan coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage reporters' knowledge of processes and actors to schedule coverage, allocate staff predictably, and ease handling of unexpected events by freeing resources in advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use typifications to regulate workflow and conserve personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers 'use typifications to transform the idiosyncratic occurrences of the everyday world into raw materials that can be subjected to routine processing and dissemination' and to 'conserve personnel and retain control of the flow of newswork.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify events into typifications (spot/developing/continuing/what-a-story) to decide staffing patterns, preassign tasks, and standardize responses so routine and extraordinary events are processed efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional stock of knowledge-at-hand (apply appropriate techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters' familiarity with how processes unfold (their 'professional stock of knowledge-at-hand') enables prediction of outcomes and selection of the appropriate reportorial techniques for different typifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate institutional knowledge (actors, committee dispositions, routine sequences) so reporters can anticipate what to look for, weigh coverage priorities, and perform with autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid objectification/reification and overreliance on typifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If typifications become 'objectified' they can be 'seductive' and lead to inaccurate collective predictions; 'inaccurately predicted events-as-news require major unplanned alterations in work processes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of taken-for-granted categories; monitor for stereotyping or inflexible application of typifications that could blind staff to novel developments and cause misjudgment of newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: "What-a-story" typification: invoke special emergency routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Inaccurately predicted or extraordinarily consequential events are processed under the special typification 'What-a-story!' which 'is constituted in the unusual arrangements that are routinely made to cope' with such a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediately institute established high-priority routines (call-in reporters, reassign beats, change page formats, invoke past comparable cases), rely on practiced roles and minimal discussion to expedite response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use past comparable events as quick decision heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoking prior 'what-a-story' cases (e.g., Coolidge analogy) alerts staff to an 'unusual routine' and reduces deliberation by referencing taken-for-granted responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep institutional memory of prior major events to guide rapid decisions about staffing, layout, and coverage when surprises occur — but avoid literal replication when context differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism and flexibility: reporters must be generalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Flexibility is accomplished by professionalism: 'Specialties are ignored when necessary. Everyone must be capable of doing everyone else's work... each specialist must be a generalist, and vice versa.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train reporters to cover multiple beats, encourage autonomy and judgement, and forego overly complex editorial micro-management so the organization can reassign people quickly in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize direct supervision; encourage autonomy to save costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Because most reporting takes place outside the newsroom and direct supervision would be expensive, 'news organizations maintain flexibility and save money by discouraging a more complex bureaucracy... and by encouraging professionalism among reporters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure organizations to empower experienced reporters, reduce layers of editorial oversight, and rely on professional norms rather than costly supervisory systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource allocation decisions depend on time/space dispersion
rubrics_metrics.description: The alternative chosen to cover an event (e.g., pay overtime, pull staff, hire freelance) 'depended upon the specific situation—the existing dispersion of both film crews and occurrences in time and space at that moment of that day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make allocation choices contingent on location, distance from newsroom, available personnel at that time, and the medium's production constraints; plan contingencies for remote/late events.
